Computable Analysis / Gaussian integrals / Improper power integrals

Finite integrals · explicit endpoint bounds · series comparison

Improper power integrals

Checked for every represented-real exponent. This includes irrational exponents and the range \(0<p<1\). The constructions use rational interval algorithms, with no Mathlib real numbers or abstract completion.

The three power tests

Lean checked
\[\int_0^1x^{-p}\,dx\simeq\frac1{1-p}\quad(p<1),\qquad \int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx\simeq\frac1{p-1}\quad(p>1).\] \[\int_0^1x^{-p}\,dx\text{ converges}\iff p<1,\qquad \int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx\text{ converges}\iff p>1.\] \[\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-p}\text{ converges}\iff p>1.\]

Strict separation from one is found in a finite input enclosure. Divergence uses weak order and therefore includes the critical exponent without deciding real equality. Any supplied improper-integral witness on the stated exhaustion agrees with the reciprocal formula.

Exact values, convergence classifications, and the integral test

Finite intervals, not a compactness theorem

“Compact integral” here means a definite integral over a finite closed rational interval away from zero. No topological compactness theorem is introduced. The exponent is an arbitrary represented real; the finite truncation endpoints are rational.

The proof starts with independently computed binomial powers. Finite polynomial integration, reflection, and a justified reciprocal substitution construct the finite integrals. Only then do endpoint bounds establish improper limits, and finite rectangles establish the series test.

\[(1-p)\int_a^b x^{-p}\,dx\simeq b^{1-p}-a^{1-p}\qquad(0<a\le b\le1).\]

The division-free identity remains valid at the critical exponent; it does not claim a separate logarithm identity. The proofs do not use an already completed zeta series to justify the integrals.

Finite intervals below one · Finite intervals above one and reciprocal substitution

A finite endpoint estimate

Computed bounds

For a rational exponent interval \(1+1/(q+1)\le s\le m+2\), set

\[B_m=(m+3)^{m+1},\quad r_q=\frac{2q+2}{2q+3},\quad K_j=(m+1)2^j,\quad a_j=\frac{2^{-j}}{1+K_jB_m}.\]

If \(J_{s,L}\) is the integrated finite binomial polynomial, the checked estimate is

\[\left|J_{s,L}(1-a)-\frac1{s-1}\right| \le 2(q+1)B_m r_q^j+2^{-j},\qquad 0\le a\le a_j,\quad L\ge K_j.\]

This finite rational inequality precedes every improper limit. It is uniform in the exponent, so it transfers to irrational inputs through their rational enclosures. Use \(s=2-p\) at zero and \(s=p\) at infinity. The public theorems use the fixed dyadic exhaustions \([2^{-(2n+1)},1]\) and \([1,2^{2n+1}]\).

Finite endpoint proof · Constructed improper limit

The series follows from the integrals

Arbitrary represented exponents

Positivity and monotonicity are proved for the power evaluator. Unit rectangles then give, for nonnegative \(p\),

\[\int_{N+1}^{M+1}x^{-p}\,dx\le \sum_{n=N+1}^M n^{-p}\le\int_N^M x^{-p}\,dx.\]

For \(p>1\), the algorithm chooses a finite truncation from the integral error and computes that finite sum to a prescribed rational width. If its rational candidate at stage \(n\) is \(c_n\), the output intersects the boxes

\[[c_j-3\cdot2^{-j},\ c_j+3\cdot2^{-j}],\qquad 0\le j\le n.\]

The boxes nest, have width at most \(6\cdot2^{-n}\), and converge to the independent partial sums. Uniqueness and invariance under changing the exponent representation are checked. This general reference algorithm has conservative, potentially very large truncations; it is not an efficient numerical zeta implementation. The earlier integer algorithms retain their sharper bounds.

Finite comparison · Series computation and representation invariance

Divergence is a finite lower bound

For \(p\le1\), the series terms dominate the harmonic terms and \(S_{2^{2T}}\ge T\). For the divergent improper integrals, dyadic harmonic rectangles each contribute lower area \(1/2\). These finite bounds exclude every finite represented limit, including at \(p=1\). Actual finite-interval integral witnesses exist on both divergent sides.

Connections still to establish

Separate work

These results supply a function-specific improper-integration example. They do not yet prove Gaussian normalization, the Gamma integral or geometric ball volume, or the continuous central limit theorem.
